title: NOT EVERYONE WHO SAYS “GOD TOLD ME” ACTUALLY HEARD FROM GOD
paragraphs: NOT EVERYONE WHO SAYS “GOD TOLD ME” ACTUALLY HEARD FROM GOD
The four words that can silence discernment, manipulate a wounded heart, and put God's signature on something He never said.
There are four words that can make a Christian stop asking questions.
Four words that can turn somebody’s private opinion into what sounds like a command from heaven.

Four words that have started relationships, ended marriages, launched ministries, justified reckless decisions, wounded churches, frightened vulnerable believers, and left sincere people wondering why God supposedly promised something that never happened.
“God told me.”
Maybe you have heard those words spoken over you.
Maybe someone looked directly into your eyes and said, “God told me you are supposed to do this.”
Maybe somebody told you whom you were going to marry.
Maybe someone said God had revealed your future.
Maybe a person told you that if you walked away from them, you were walking away from God.
Maybe a preacher announced that God had guaranteed something Scripture never guaranteed.
Or perhaps this article is uncomfortable for a different reason.
Maybe you have said those words yourself.
And maybe, if you are painfully honest, you are no longer certain that God actually said what you claimed He said.
Stay with me.
Because this is not an attack on the Holy Spirit.

This is not an argument that God is distant, silent, powerless, or unable to guide His children. Scripture teaches the reality and activity of the Holy Spirit. Jesus said His sheep hear His voice and follow Him. The Spirit glorifies Christ and guides believers in truth.
The danger is not believing that God speaks.
The danger is believing that everything presented as God's voice must therefore be God's voice.
Those are not the same thing.
And the Bible itself commands us to know the difference.
John writes:
“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits…”
—1 John 4:1
That Greek expression is devastatingly clear.
Μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε — mē panti pneumati pisteuete.
Do not believe every spirit.
Then comes the command:
δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα — dokimazete ta pneumata.
Test the spirits.
The verb dokimazō carries the idea of examining or testing something to determine its genuineness.
Notice what John does not say.
He does not say, “If someone sounds spiritual, believe them.”
He does not say, “If they are confident, believe them.”
He does not say, “If they have a large ministry, believe them.”
He does not say, “If they cry while saying it, believe them.”
He does not say, “If you get goosebumps, believe them.”
He says:
Test.
That means biblical discernment is not unbelief.
Discernment is obedience.
You are not dishonoring the Holy Spirit when you test something by the truth God has already revealed. You are obeying the Holy Spirit-inspired Scriptures when you do.
And this problem did not begin with social media prophets.
Long before microphones, livestreams, conference stages, viral reels, and charismatic personalities existed, God confronted people who were putting His name behind their own words.
Jeremiah records one of Scripture's most sobering rebukes of false prophetic claims.
God describes prophets proclaiming lies in His name and crying:
“חָלַמְתִּי חָלָמְתִּי”
ḥālamtî, ḥālamtî.
“I have dreamed! I have dreamed!”
—Jeremiah 23:25
Then God exposes something terrifying.
Their messages were coming from what Jeremiah describes as the deceit of their own hearts.
Think about that.
A person can be deeply convinced…
emotionally stirred…
religiously sincere…
and still mistake what is arising from within themselves for something God has spoken.
That should humble every one of us.
Because sometimes what we call “God told me” may actually mean:
“I desperately want this.”
“I am afraid of losing this.”
“This makes sense to me.”
“I had a powerful emotional experience.”
“I had a dream.”
“I felt strongly about it.”
“I heard somebody else say something similar.”
“I cannot explain this feeling.”
None of those things automatically means God did not lead you.
But none of them automatically means He did.

There is an enormous difference between saying, “I sense the Lord may be leading me here, and I want to test this biblically,” and declaring, “God told me,” as though your interpretation carries the authority of Scripture.
One posture is humble.
The other can become spiritually dangerous.
Because once someone places the words “God told me” in front of a personal opinion, disagreement suddenly feels like rebellion against God.
Imagine a young woman hearing:
“God told me you're supposed to marry me.”
What happens if she does not want to?
Now she is not merely rejecting a man's proposal.
She has been made to feel as though she is rejecting God's will.
Imagine a church member hearing:
“God told me you need to give this amount.”
Imagine a wounded spouse hearing:
“God told me our marriage is finished,” when the speaker is using divine language to bypass biblical responsibility.
Imagine someone terrified because a stranger confidently predicted tragedy over their family.
Imagine a believer being told:
“If you leave this ministry, you're leaving God's covering.”
This is why claiming divine authority is serious.
God's name is not punctuation for our preferences.

And Scripture shows just how seriously God takes people speaking presumptuously in His name. Deuteronomy 18 warns against the prophet who speaks a word God did not command. It also tells Israel that when a supposed prediction spoken in God's name fails, they are not to fear the speaker.
That last part matters.
You do not have to live imprisoned by failed prophecies.
You do not have to spend ten years terrified because somebody told you God said something would happen.
You do not have to force circumstances to fulfill another person's prediction.
You do not have to marry somebody because they said God selected you.
You do not have to remain under spiritual manipulation because someone attached God's name to their demands.
You belong to Jesus Christ.
And Jesus did not rescue you from darkness so another human being could control your conscience by pretending to possess unquestionable access to God's private instructions for your life.
But there is another side to this.
And it may hurt more.
Sometimes the person misusing “God told me” is not a manipulative preacher.
Sometimes it is us.
Sometimes we want something so badly that we baptize desire as revelation.
We want the relationship.
God told me.
We want the job.
God told me.
We want to leave.
God told me.
We want to stay.
God told me.
We want the ministry.
God told me.
We dislike somebody's correction.
God told me they're jealous.
We do not want accountability.
God told me I don't need anyone's approval.
And suddenly God seems to agree with everything we already wanted.
That should make us tremble.
Not because Christians must live paralyzed, terrified of making decisions.
But because humility before God is safer than pretending certainty we do not possess.
Sometimes one of the most spiritually mature sentences you can say is:
“I believe God may be leading me, but I could be wrong.”
There is no shame in that sentence.
There is humility in it.
The apostles themselves commended examination.
When Paul preached in Berea, Acts 17:11 tells us that the Bereans received the message eagerly while “examining the Scriptures daily” to determine whether what they were hearing was true.
Think about who they were checking.
Paul.
The apostle Paul.
They did not say, “He's an apostle, so asking questions would dishonor him.”
They searched the Scriptures.
And Scripture praises them for it.
The Greek describes them as:
ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς — anakrinontes tas graphas.
Examining the Scriptures.
Christian faith was never intended to require shutting down your mind whenever a religious person speaks confidently.
Open your Bible.
Examine.
Pray.
Seek wise counsel.
Look at the fruit.
Look at the context.
Ask whether what you are hearing agrees with God's revealed character and Word.
And above everything else…
look at Jesus.
Because the Holy Spirit does not exist to make human personalities impressive.
Jesus said concerning the Spirit:
“He will glorify Me.”
—John 16:14
That gives us a beautiful center of gravity.
The Spirit's ministry exalts Christ.
So when supposed revelation consistently produces obsession with a messenger rather than worship of Jesus, something has gone terribly wrong.
When the personality becomes untouchable…
when questioning the leader becomes equivalent to questioning God…
when every disagreement receives a convenient “God told me”…
when failed predictions disappear without repentance…
when fear keeps people loyal…
when Scripture is twisted to protect the speaker…
when Jesus becomes almost secondary to revelations, personalities, experiences, money, power, and spectacle…
do not surrender your discernment.
Test.
Because spectacular does not automatically mean spiritual.
Paul's warning in Galatians goes even further.
He essentially tells the church that even if an angel from heaven proclaimed a gospel contrary to the one already received, that messenger was to be rejected.
Let that settle into your heart.
Even an extraordinary supernatural claim does not outrank the Gospel.
Not a dream.
Not a vision.
Not an angelic claim.
Not a prophecy.
Not a famous preacher.
Not your favorite Christian creator.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not me.
Jesus Christ and the truth He has revealed must remain above every human messenger.
That is why you should never believe something merely because we publish it.
Open your Bible.
Check the context.
Test what we say.
If we ever point you away from Jesus Christ, reject what we say.
If we ever teach a gospel contrary to the apostolic Gospel, reject what we say.
If we ever ask you to treat our voice as though it carries the authority of Scripture, reject that demand.
A Christian ministry should never be afraid of an open Bible.
And there is something else we desperately need to recover.
Repentance when we get it wrong.
Perhaps you once told somebody, “God told me,” and later realized it may have been your own desire.
You do not need to hide.
You can repent.
Maybe you frightened somebody with a prediction.
You can apologize.
Maybe you manipulated someone by attaching God's authority to what you wanted.
Confess it.
Maybe you were deceived by someone else's supposed word from God and now feel foolish.
Come back to Christ.
Grace is waiting.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not go to the cross only for respectable sins.
He died for our religious pride too.
He died for our manipulation.
Our presumption.
Our dishonesty.
Our hunger to appear spiritually important.
Our desperate need to be right.
Our secret craving to be seen as somebody who has a special connection with heaven.
At Calvary, the masks come off.
There is no celebrity prophet at the foot of the cross.
No impressive Christian.
No spiritual superstar.
Only sinners who need mercy.
And Christ gives mercy.
The Gospel does not say, “Pretend you never got anything wrong.”
The Gospel says repent and believe.
Bring your mistakes into the light.
Bring your false certainty.
Bring the words you should never have spoken in God's name.
Bring the decisions you made from fear.
Bring the wounds left by spiritual manipulation.
Bring your confusion.
Bring your embarrassment.
Bring all of it to Jesus.
Because Jesus specializes in taking the places where sin wrote shame and rewriting them with grace.
That is our heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps somebody reading this right now is carrying a wound nobody sees.
Somebody once told you, “God said…”
And you obeyed because you were afraid not to.
Then everything collapsed.
Now you do not know whom to trust.
Maybe you do not even trust yourself anymore.
Hear this carefully:
A human being misrepresenting God does not mean God misrepresented Himself.
People can fail you.
Leaders can fail you.
Christ does not.
Someone can misuse Scripture.
Scripture is not therefore false.
Someone can lie in God's name.
God does not therefore become a liar.
Do not let somebody else's counterfeit voice steal your hunger for the real Shepherd.
Return to Jesus.
Return to His Word.
Learn His character.
Become so rooted in Scripture that spiritual-sounding manipulation becomes harder to sell to you.
And when you do believe the Lord is leading you personally, hold that conviction with reverence and humility.
You do not need to make God your accomplice to win an argument.
You do not need “God told me” to make your opinion impressive.
Sometimes “I believe…”
“I sense…”
“I am praying…”
“I think wisdom is leading me…”
“I could be mistaken…”
are profoundly Christian sentences.
Humility does not weaken genuine faith.
It protects us from confusing ourselves with God.
Stay here for a moment.
Ask Jesus:
“Lord, have I ever used Your name to strengthen something You never said?”
And listen.
Maybe there is someone you need to apologize to.
Maybe there is a prediction you need to stop fearing.
Maybe there is a relationship where spiritual language has been used to control you.
Maybe there is a teacher you have been treating as unquestionable.
Maybe there is simply a deeper hunger rising in you:
“Jesus, teach me to recognize truth.”
Not because typing a phrase saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light is where honesty begins.
And please do not turn this article into ammunition for attacking every Christian who says they believe God led them.
That would miss the point completely.
The goal is not cynicism.
The goal is discernment.
The goal is not mocking spiritual gifts.
The goal is biblical faithfulness.
The goal is not becoming suspicious of everyone.
The goal is becoming deeply anchored in Christ.
Strong feelings are real feelings.
But strong feelings are not Scripture.
Send it privately to the person recovering from spiritual manipulation.
Grace cannot be bought.
But generosity and practical support can help Christian ministry continue.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with following the Messiah.
Ministries are servants.
Jesus is Lord.
And the safest place for your soul will never be beneath the unquestionable voice of a human personality.
It will be at the feet of Jesus, with your Bible open, your heart humble, your sins confessed, your discernment awake, and your eyes fixed on Christ.
Because someday you may discover that the most dangerous spiritual sentence was not spoken by an obvious enemy.
It came from someone you trusted.
Perhaps even from your own lips.
“God told me.”
So test it.
Bring it beneath Scripture.
Bring it before Jesus.
And never be afraid to discover that God did not say what a human being claimed He said.
Because God's truth does not need our exaggeration.
His Word does not need our manipulation.
And Jesus does not need counterfeit authority to change a human heart.
Never let someone else's “God told me” become louder in your soul than what God has actually revealed in His Word.
